hints: Focus on what is actually given to you in passive immunity: ready-made antibodies, not the cells or instructions to make your own.
Remember that antibodies are proteins in the blood, and your body does not make memory cells during passive immunity, so think about what happens when those proteins are used up.
walkthrough:
**Recall what passive immunity means**

Passive immunity means you receive ready-made antibodies from elsewhere, for example across the placenta or in an antiserum injection. You do not make them yourself.

Think: no antigen exposure, no activation of your own B cells.

**Ask why the protection cannot last**

Antibodies are protein molecules circulating in plasma. Like all proteins, they are naturally broken down by enzymes over days to weeks.

Key rule: no memory B cells are formed, so there is nothing to replace them.

**Link to the short time effect**

Once those donated antibodies are broken down, protection disappears. There is no secondary response possible because your immune system never learned the pathogen.

So the cause is loss of the antibodies themselves, which is option A.

options.A: Correct. The donated antibodies are proteins that are soon metabolised and broken down, and with no memory cells to make more, immunity is short lived.
options.B: Antigens are not injected in passive immunity, only antibodies are, so breakdown of antigens does not explain the short protection.
options.C: No memory cells are made at all in passive immunity, so they cannot be the thing that dies to end protection.
options.D: Phagocytes are long lived cells made continuously by bone marrow, and their lifespan is not the reason passive immunity fades.
